extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century London public (coffeehouse readers, gentlemen and ladies interested in morals and taste)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the proper use and limits of wit, lampoon, and ridicule in moral and social writing, together with related norms of taste (monuments/epitaphs, polite company, hypochondria). Aims to instruct essayists and polite readers about humane, tasteful, and reasonable conduct in satire and public representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid secret stabs to reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The giving of secret stabs to a man's reputation (anonymous lampoons and satyrs) betrays a base, ungenerous spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lampoons and satyrs written with wit and spirit are compared to 'poison'd Darts' that not only wound but make the wound incurable. Do not publish anonymous attacks that expose private persons to secret shame or sorrow; measure injury by the feelings of the person who receives it, not by the giver's notion of harmlessness. Examples: general condemnation of malicious lampooners who expose innocent families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper wit with virtue and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and ridicule must be tempered with virtue and humanity; untempered wit is pernicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making Virtue, Merit, or other praise-worthy qualities the subject of ridicule and buffoonry. When wit lacks humanity it can render humane persons ridiculous and produce long-lasting harm. The essay states: 'So pernicious a thing is Wit, when it is not tempered with Virtue and Humanity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer generous civil responses to satire
rubrics_metrics.description: A generous, civil treatment of those who lampoon you is an effective and honorable way to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Julius Caesar invited Catullus to supper and made him a friend; Cardinal Mazarin treated Quillet with civility and later rewarded him, which led the poet to expunge offending passages and dedicate a later edition to the Cardinal. The advice: answer ridicule with civility and moderation rather than vengeance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cruel, disproportionate punishments of satirists
rubrics_metrics.description: Severe, barbarous punishments for satirical speech are improper and shocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Pasquinade incident—when the satirist revealed himself the Pope rewarded him but then ordered mutilation (tongue cut out, hands chopped off). The essay implies such reprisals are barbarous and unjust. Do not employ cruelty to silence satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that satire wounds even when met with outward composure
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who seem untroubled by ridicule may still be inwardly wounded; not showing resentment does not mean no injury was done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Socrates attended and bore Aristophanes's ridicule publicly, but the essay suggests that it made an impression on him. Writers should recognize the private anguish lampoons can produce even when the target appears philosophically resigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attacking the innocent and private; choose worthy targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make private persons, families, or the innocent the object of satire and ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'innocent young Lady' or a 'Father of a Family' should not be exposed for minor faults or misinterpreted actions; satirists should focus on appropriate objects (e.g., public vice or folly) rather than private domestic matters that cause needless shame and sorrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of authorial disposition: indiscretion and malice differ but both are harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Both heedless (indiscreet) writers and ill-natured writers do harm, though in different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An indiscreet writer may hurt by careless exposure or silly ambition for raillery; an ill-natured writer injures indiscriminately. The essay counsels authors to avoid both heedless levity and malicious intent: 'an indiscreet Man is more hurtful than an ill-natured one...the other injures indifferently both Friends and Foes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness and distance as remedies for impertinent company
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with impertinent or ill-suited company, maintain polite distance and formalities rather than intimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in letters: advise keeping visits strictly formal ('let me beg of you never to make me any more Visits'—i.e., know people by sight only), preserve decorum in conversation, and avoid encouraging those 'not fit for the better sort of Conversation' to intrude on refined company. Practical guidance: acknowledge acquaintances courteously but limit intimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monuments and epitaphs should reflect true character and fit the person
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorials (monuments, inscriptions) ought to match the real character and achievements of the person commemorated; avoid extravagant or inappropriate praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Sir Cloudesly Shovel's monument: instead of representing a rough English admiral, it shows a beau in a periwig and meaningless panegyric. Advice: have inscriptions and monuments reviewed by men of learning and genius before execution; use appropriate symbols (e.g., naval ornaments for admirals) and avoid lofty but empty language or excessive flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from better taste abroad — use appropriate, intelligible forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign examples (Dutch monuments) often show superior taste in representing persons with appropriate symbols and clearer antiquarian sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cites Dutch admirals' monuments adorned with rostral crowns, seaweed, shells, and coral as better matched to the subject. Ensure public memorials convey intelligible and relevant information about the person's public deeds rather than mere stylistic display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make the preservation of life the sole aim; avoid hypochondriacal regimen
rubrics_metrics.description: The preservation of life should be a secondary concern to the direction and enjoyment of life; excessive fear of death and rigid regimens are harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of the valetudinarian who measures food, sleep, and perspiration precisely: 'To consult the Preservation of Life, as the only End of it...are Purposes so abject, so mean, so unworthy human Nature.' Practical guidance: take due care of health but avoid groundless fears, melancholy apprehensions, and micromanagement that ruin the pleasures and duties of life. Cultivate cheerfulness and capacity for business as part of preserving health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow natural solicitations rather than slavish rules for health
rubrics_metrics.description: Govern bodily needs (hunger, thirst, sleep, exercise) by natural feeling rather than slavishly by bookish prescriptions or mechanical devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: the man who lives 'in a Pair of Scales' and times meals and sleep exactly by his chair's weighing. Instead, respond to natural appetites and preserve mental cheerfulness; avoid making regimen the central object so as to destroy the enjoyment of life.
